whatItDoes: Would make Bothell part of the Shoreline Fire Department Regional Fire Authority on March 1, 2027, under the amended regional fire plan in Resolution 1784. Bothell’s fire department would join the regional authority, while current fire and emergency medical service levels would continue. Bothell would have representation on the authority’s board, and its voters would vote on the authority’s future ballot measures, including taxes and benefit charges.
yesMeans: A YES vote would approve Bothell’s annexation into the regional fire authority under this plan.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject this annexation proposal.

whatItDoes: Would increase Clyde Hill’s regular property tax levy rate from about $0.30 to no more than $0.50 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027 to fund police, fire, emergency medical, 911 dispatch, land-use and zoning services. The total levy amount could then rise by a 3% annual limit factor in 2028–2036, and the 2036 levy would become the base for later years. Qualifying seniors, veterans and people with disabilities would be exempt from the increase. The city estimates the 2027 increase at about $225 for a property assessed at $1 million.
yesMeans: A YES vote would approve the higher 2027 levy, the 3% annual increase limit for 2028–2036, and use of the 2036 levy as the later tax base.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject these proposed levy changes.

whatItDoes: Would authorize Issaquah to borrow up to $18 million through general obligation bonds, repaid within 20 years through annual additional property taxes. The money would fund sports fields and courts, new trails and trailhead improvements, restoration of Confluence Park’s Ek House, playground improvements, a new dog park and related park and recreation projects. The city plans to issue these as earlier park bonds retire and estimates an average cost of about $80 a year for a $1 million home. Existing qualifying exemptions for low-income seniors, certain veterans and others would continue.
yesMeans: A YES vote would authorize the park and recreation bonds and property taxes to repay them.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject this bond and repayment-tax authorization.

whatItDoes: Would increase Kenmore’s maximum regular property tax rate to $1.25 per $1,000 of assessed value for collection in 2027, funding climate and environmental programs, affordable housing and human services. It would allow the levy amount to rise by up to 6% annually in 2028–2032, subject to the state-law maximum rate, and use the 2032 levy as the base for future levies. Qualifying seniors, veterans and others would be exempt from the increase. The city estimates an added cost of about $30 a month for a home assessed at $1 million.
yesMeans: A YES vote would approve this property tax increase, the subsequent annual levy increases and the new levy base.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject these proposed levy changes.

whatItDoes: Would temporarily increase Lake Forest Park’s regular property tax levy for public safety, including police, safety equipment, 911 dispatch, emergency management, jail services and mental health crisis response. The maximum total regular levy rate would be $0.88920 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2027. The increase could rise with Seattle-area consumer-price inflation for the next five years, 2028–2032, after a public process and council vote. When it expires, the levy would return to what it would have been without this increase. Qualifying low-income seniors, disabled veterans and other people with disabilities would be exempt. The city estimates the increase at $0.22 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027.
yesMeans: A YES vote would approve this temporary public-safety property tax increase and its inflation adjustments.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject this levy increase.

whatItDoes: Would raise Milton’s sales and use tax by 0.1 percentage point beginning in 2027, adding 10 cents to a taxable $100 purchase. Revenue would provide ongoing funding for police and other public-safety purposes allowed by state law, including law-enforcement staffing. The city would have to share 15% of these tax proceeds with the county.
yesMeans: A YES vote would approve this sales and use tax increase for public safety.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject the proposed tax increase.

whatItDoes: Would raise SeaTac’s sales and use tax by 0.1 percentage point to fund fire protection and prevention, emergency medical response, law-enforcement staffing, criminal justice, public-safety operations and other city services allowed by law. This would add 10 cents to a taxable $100 purchase. The city would receive 85% of the revenue and King County 15%; at least one-third would have to fund fire protection, criminal justice, or both. Most groceries, motor-vehicle sales and the first 36 months of vehicle leases would be exempt from this tax.
yesMeans: A YES vote would authorize this sales and use tax increase with the stated revenue-sharing and spending requirements.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject the proposed tax increase.

whatItDoes: Would create a Shoreline Metropolitan Park District with the same boundaries as the city and a governing board made up of city councilmembers. It would fund a new indoor pool facility and possible future recreational facilities, including construction, operation, maintenance, renovation and expansion. Revenue could be used only for those facilities, rather than other city needs. The district could levy property taxes up to $0.75 per $1,000 of assessed value; the anticipated starting rate is $0.55, or the amount needed to raise about $8.8 million a year. Collection would begin in 2028.
yesMeans: A FOR vote would create the park district with these taxing and recreation-facility powers.
noMeans: An AGAINST vote would reject creation of this park district.

whatItDoes: Would authorize Auburn School District to borrow up to $491 million through general obligation bonds, repaid within 20 years through annual additional property taxes. The money would build and equip a new middle school and larger replacement schools for Cascade Middle School and Alpac Elementary, with safety, technology, energy-efficiency and playfield improvements. The district expects about $36,248,500 in state construction assistance if voters approve. A property tax exemption may be available to qualifying senior or disabled homeowners.
yesMeans: An APPROVED vote would authorize the school-construction bonds and property taxes to repay them.
noMeans: A REJECTED vote would reject this bond and repayment-tax authorization.

whatItDoes: Would authorize Highline School District to borrow $595.4 million through general obligation bonds, repaid within 21 years through annual additional property taxes. It would replace Cascade and Sylvester middle schools, partly rebuild and modernize Chinook Middle School, and rebuild the former Southern Heights Elementary site for CHOICE Academy. It would also fund building-system, security, fire-system, earthquake-safety and accessibility work across the district, plus design plans for Valley View Early Learning Center and Hilltop Elementary. Qualifying homeowners may be eligible for property tax exemptions.
yesMeans: An APPROVED vote would authorize these school-construction and safety bonds and property taxes to repay them.
noMeans: A REJECTED vote would reject this bond and repayment-tax authorization.

whatItDoes: Would authorize Highline School District to collect an additional $12 million in property taxes each year from 2027 through 2030 for educational technology, programs and staff, and capital improvements not funded by the state. Work includes cybersecurity, internet and technology infrastructure, student and staff devices, instructional software, training, and school-facility improvements. Estimated rates per $1,000 of assessed value are $0.36 in 2027, $0.35 in 2028, $0.34 in 2029 and $0.32 in 2030; actual rates would depend on assessed values. Qualifying homeowners may be eligible for exemptions.
yesMeans: A YES vote would authorize this four-year technology and capital-improvements levy.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject this levy authorization.

whatItDoes: Would replace Kent School District’s levy that expires in 2027 with property taxes for educational programs and operating costs not paid for by the state’s basic-education program. Collections would be $104.7 million in 2028, $111.1 million in 2029, $115.7 million in 2030 and $121.4 million in 2031. Estimated rates per $1,000 of assessed value are $1.95, $1.93, $1.88 and $1.84 respectively. The money would support day-to-day operations, including counselors, learning and career programs, transportation, safety, athletics, extracurricular activities and classroom support. Qualifying senior or disabled homeowners may be eligible for an exemption.
yesMeans: A YES vote would authorize this replacement school-programs and operations levy for 2028–2031.
noMeans: A NO vote would reject this replacement levy.
